title: Integrated control of Na transport along the nephron
journal: Clinical Journal of the American Society of Nephrology
funder: L.G. Palmer: National Institutes of Health grant R01-DK27847. J. Schnermann: Intramural Research Program of the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases.
result: Review. More than 500 g of sodium is filtered daily; under most conditions the kidneys excrete more than 95% of ingested sodium. The proximal tubule reabsorbs 60-70% (apical NHE3 the main mechanism), the ascending loop of Henle, mostly the thick limb, 25-30% (NKCC2 and NHE3), and the distal convoluted tubule and collecting ducts no more than 5-10%, through thiazide-sensitive NCC (early DCT) and amiloride-sensitive ENaC (late DCT, connecting tubule, collecting duct); distal reabsorption is the regulated part. Two-thirds or more of renal oxygen uptake is spent on the Na,K-ATPase. With plausible tenfold changes in intake, fractional reabsorption varies between about 97% and 99.7%. Sodium depletion increases ENaC activity, an effect mimicked by aldosterone. Potassium loading lowers NCC phosphorylation and abundance and raises ENaC activity, shifting sodium reabsorption to segments where principal cells secrete K+ in exchange for Na+. Changes in body Na content and blood volume are the likely cause of the relation between Na intake and blood pressure.
